title: CFP opens 30-day negotiating window with ESPN on 24-team playoff expansion
dek: College Football Playoff officials triggered a mandatory negotiating period with ESPN on September 8 to discuss media rights for a potential 24-team playoff format beginning in 2027. The move signals serious exploration of expansion, though the CFP statement emphasizes this is not yet a commitment. A December 1 deadline looms for final decisions on format and conference championship games.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The CFP triggered a 30-day negotiating window with ESPN on September 8, 2026, over a potential 24-team playoff expansion, with a final decision deadline of December 1.
bottom_line: The December 1 deadline for format and conference championship decisions will determine whether expansion gains sufficient support from the Big Ten and SEC, whose combined weight controls the outcome per the CFP's governance structure. If talks collapse and rights go to market, the distribution of playoff games across multiple networks would represent a fundamental shift in how college football's postseason is sold and broadcast.
body: The College Football Playoff triggered a mandatory 30-day negotiating window with ESPN on Tuesday, September 8, beginning formal discussions on expanding the playoff to 24 teams in 2027. The move marks the first substantive step toward a format shift that would eliminate conference championship games, reshape the bowl schedule, and require ESPN to account for the loss of at least $200 million in annual media value from those games, according to ESPN's reporting.

The CFP's statement tempers expectations: "This does not represent a decision or commitment to expand, but rather an opportunity to engage with ESPN and gather additional information to help determine a path forward." The window gives ESPN and the CFP until December 1 to reach agreement on revised media rights. On that same date, conferences must notify their broadcast partners whether they intend to drop conference championship games, a procedural link that ties format decisions to scheduling and media revenue across the sport.

The 24-team format that has garnered the most support among playoff officials would consist of the 23 highest-ranked teams plus one spot reserved for a Group of Five school, according to reporting from Yahoo Sports cited by Awful Announcing. The top eight teams would receive byes. The playoff would likely begin the second weekend of December, with eight first-round games played on campus followed by a second round of eight home games the following week. All quarterfinals, both semifinals, and the national championship would remain under ESPN's control under the current contract, plus the first two newly added games. If the playoff expands beyond 14 teams, any additional games beyond those would be subject to ESPN's exclusive right of first negotiation with the CFP.

SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey has outlined requirements he would accept for a 24-team field: teams must play at least 10 qualifying events against power conference opponents or Notre Dame to be eligible for playoff inclusion, per Ross Dellenger's reporting in Yahoo Sports. This criterion would effectively exclude Group of Five schools except for the one designated spot. The requirement would necessitate changes to Big Ten scheduling, as that conference does not currently mandate nonconference games against power opponents, though Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti, who initiated the expansion discussion in February, has reportedly expressed openness to Sankey's framework.

The SEC has remained skeptical of 24-team expansion. In previous remarks, Sankey noted that models suggested his league would receive only marginal benefit from the format, and the SEC's official position has favored a 16-team field. By contrast, the ACC and Big 12 have both united behind the 24-team option. ESPN previously proposed a 20-team format to the committee, which rejected the idea.

Under the contract triggered this week, ESPN must present its best offer to the CFP within 30 days, accounting for the strong possibility of expansion and the presumed loss of conference championship game revenue. If the parties do not reach agreement, the CFP can shop the additional games to the open market, though ESPN retains matching rights and guaranteed control of the core playoff games. When the playoff expanded to 12 teams, ESPN was the only network that submitted a bid.
